chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.summary: Before the arrival of the Europeans, the lands that now constitute Brazil were inhabited and settled by diverse tribes for thousands of years. The Portuguese landed in the so-called "New World" on April 22, 1500, commanded by Pedro Álvares Cabral, an explorer on his way to India under the sponsorship of the Kingdom of Portugal and the support of the Catholic Church.

events.text: The country expanded south along the coast and west along the Amazon River and other inland rivers from the original 15 hereditary captaincy colonies established on the northeast Atlantic coast east of the Tordesillas Line, an imaginary line in the form of a treaty signed in 1494 that divided the Portuguese domain to the east from the Spanish domain to the west.

The Portuguese landed in the so-called "New World" on April 22, 1500, commanded by Pedro Álvares Cabral, an explorer on his way to India under the sponsorship of the Kingdom of Portugal and the support of the Catholic Church.
On September 7, 1822, prince regent Pedro declared Brazil's independence from Portugal and so the Kingdom of Brazil became the Empire of Brazil, in which he became its first emperor.

events.label: 19th c.
events.text: Between the 16th to the early 19th century, Brazil was created and expanded as a colony, kingdom, and an integral part of the Portuguese Empire.
In 1889, a military coup toppled the monarchy and the First Brazilian Republic was established, albeit with the first five years of the republic as a military dictatorship.
Growing political instability within the republic brought its downfall in 1930, when a military coup headed by Getúlio Vargas overthrew the republic.
In 1945, Vargas' was deposed, and from 1945 to 1964, democracy was briefly restored in the Fourth Brazilian Republic.

events.label: 20th c.
events.text: The country's borders were only finalized in the early 20th century, with most of the expansion occurring before the independence, resulting in the largest contiguous territory in the Americas.
In 1964, with support from the United States, another military dictatorship was established through a military coup.
Under President Emílio Garrastazu Médici's tenure, from 1969 to 1974, Brazil experienced what has been called the "Brazilian Miracle".

chapters.narrative: Before the arrival of Europeans, the lands that now constitute Brazil were inhabited and settled by diverse tribes for thousands of years [S1]. The Portuguese landed in the so-called "New World" on April 22, 1500, commanded by Pedro Álvares Cabral on his way to India under the sponsorship of the Kingdom of Portugal and the support of the Catholic Church [S1]. The country expanded from 15 hereditary captaincy colonies established east of the Tordesillas Line of 1494 along the coast and inland rivers, and between the 16th to early 19th century became part of the Portuguese Empire [S1]. Prince regent Pedro declared independence on September 7, 1822, creating the Empire of Brazil [S1]. The excerpts reflect a colonial perspective focused on Portuguese actions [S1].

chapters.title: Pre-Cabraline history
chapters.summary: Some of the earliest human remains found in the Americas, Luzia Woman, were found in the area of Pedro Leopoldo, Minas Gerais and provide evidence of human habitation going back at least 11,000 years. When Portuguese explorers arrived in Brazil, the region was inhabited by hundreds of different native tribes, "the earliest going back at least 10,000 years in the highlands of Minas Gerais".

events.text: For this reason, very little is known about the history of Brazil before 1500.

In the 1980s, another American archaeologist, Anna Curtenius Roosevelt, led excavations and geophysical surveys of the mound Teso dos Bichos.

chapters.title: Early Brazil
chapters.summary: In 1493 the papal bull inter caetera divided claims to the New World territories between Spain and Portugal and was revised in 1494 by the Treaty of Tordesillas which moved the dividing line further west. In late 1499 part of the expedition led by Alonso de Ojeda, in which Amerigo Vespucci took part, sighted Brazil.

events.label: 16th c.
events.text: Forced to defend against repeated attacks by Portuguese colonial power, the warriors of Palmares were experts in capoeira, a martial arts form developed in Brazil by African slaves in the 16th century.

This lack of interest allowed traders, pirates, and privateers of several countries to poach profitable Brazilwood in lands claimed by Portugal, with France setting up the short-lived colony of France Antarctique in 1555.
In 1578, the young King Sebastian, King of Portugal disappeared in a crusade in Morocco, during the Battle of Alcácer Quibir.

Since he had no direct heirs, Philip II of Spain, who was his uncle (and whose grandfather was the Portuguese King Manuel I of Portugal), was the only successor and took control of the Portuguese administration in 1580.
Dutch privateers began by plundering the coast: they sacked Bahia in 1604, and even temporarily captured the capital Salvador.
On February 6, 1694, after 67 years of ceaseless conflict with the cafuzos (Maroons) of Palmares, the Portuguese succeeded in destroying Cerca do Macaco, the republic's central settlement.
A system of bids for the right to extract diamonds was established, but in 1771, it was abolished and the crown retained the monopoly.
When the Portuguese monarchy fled Iberia to Brazil in 1808 during the Napoleonic wars, one of the first acts of the monarch was to open Brazilian ports to foreign ships.
Slave rebellions were frequent until the practice of slavery was abolished in 1888.

chapters.title: Kingdom and Empire of Brazil
chapters.summary: Brazil was one of only three modern states in the Americas to have a monarchy—the other two being Mexico and Haiti—for almost 90 years. As the Haitian Revolution for independence against the French crown was taking place in the late 1700s, Brazil, then a colony of Portugal, was also on the verge of starting its own revolution for independence.

events.text: As the Haitian Revolution for independence against the French crown was taking place in the late 1700s, Brazil, then a colony of Portugal, was also on the verge of starting its own revolution for independence.

In 1808, the Portuguese court, fleeing from Napoleon's invasion of Portugal during the Peninsular War in a large fleet escorted by British men-of-war, moved the government apparatus to its then-colony, Brazil, establishing themselves in the city of Rio de Janeiro.
In 1815, the king vested Brazil with the dignity of a united kingdom with Portugal and the Algarves.

They were also engaged in a number of wars fought in the region of La Plata river: the Cisplatine War (in the second half of the 1820s), the Platine War (in the 1850s), the Uruguayan War, and the Paraguayan War (in the 1860s).

Brazil's territorial dimensions as a nation were largely established before independence by the Portuguese-Brazilian monarchy (House of Bragança) in 1822, with later some territorial expansion and disputes with neighboring Spanish ex-colonies.
Brazil's independence was recognized with the Treaty of Rio de Janeiro in 1825.

From 1889 to 1930, although the country was formally a constitutional democracy, the First Republican Constitution, created in 1891, established that women and the illiterate (then the majority of the population) were prevented from voting.

In this period, known as the Third Republic, Vargas faced internally the Constitutionalist Revolt in 1932 and two separate coup d'état attempts: by Communists in 1935 and by local right-wing elements of the Brazilian Integralism movement in 1938.

In the 1950s after Vargas' second period (this time, democratically elected), the country experienced an economic boom during Juscelino Kubitschek's years, during which the capital was moved from Rio de Janeiro to Brasília.
The country's name became the Republic of the United States of Brazil (which in 1967 was changed to Federative Republic of Brazil).

chapters.narrative: Brazil was one of only three modern states in the Americas to have a monarchy for almost 90 years, the other two being Mexico and Haiti [S4]. As the Haitian Revolution for independence against the French crown was taking place in the late 1700s, Brazil, then a colony of Portugal, was also on the verge of starting its own revolution for independence [S4]. In 1808 the Portuguese court, fleeing from Napoleon's invasion of Portugal during the Peninsular War, moved the government apparatus to Rio de Janeiro [S4]. In 1815 the king vested Brazil with the dignity of a united kingdom with Portugal and the Algarves [S4]. Brazil's territorial dimensions as a nation were largely established before independence by the Portuguese-Brazilian monarchy in 1822, with its independence recognized with the Treaty of Rio de Janeiro in 1825 [S4]. The excerpts only reflect a colonial and Portuguese monarchical point of view.

chapters.title: Sixth Republic (1985–present)
chapters.summary: Tancredo Neves was elected president in an indirect election in 1985 as the nation returned to civilian rule. He died before being sworn in, and the elected vice president, José Sarney, was sworn in as president in his place.

events.text: Tancredo Neves was elected president in an indirect election in 1985 as the nation returned to civilian rule.

Fernando Collor de Mello was the first elected president by popular vote after the military regime in December 1989 defeating Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in a two-round presidential race and 35 million votes.
Reelected in 1998, he guided Brazil through a wave of financial crises.
On 1 January 2003, Lula was sworn in as the first-ever elected leftist President of Brazil.
Lula was re-elected President in the general elections of October 2006.
In the 2010 presidential election, the PT candidate was Dilma Rousseff.
Rousseff won and assumed office on January 1, 2011, as the country's first female president.
In October 2018, far-right congressman and former army captain Jair Bolsonaro was elected President of Brazil, disrupting sixteen years of continuous left-wing rule by the Worker's Party (PT).
In 2021, the second year of the pandemic, the Brazilian Senate created a parliamentary inquiry commission (CPI, in Portuguese) to investigate President Bolsonaro's conduct of the pandemic.
On January 1, 2023, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva returned to the office of the presidency, becoming the 39th president of Brazil.

Fernando Collor de Mello was the first elected president by popular vote after the military regime in December 1989 defeating Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in a two-round presidential race and 35 million votes [S5]. On 1 January 2003, Lula was sworn in as the first-ever elected leftist President of Brazil and was re-elected in October 2006 [S5]. Rousseff won and assumed office on January 1, 2011, as the country's first female president [S5]. On January 1, 2023, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva returned to the office of the presidency, becoming the 39th president of Brazil [S5].
